title: The New Creation
range: Revelation 21 to 22, with 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 8

summary.younger: One day Jesus will come back and make everything new. God will live with his people, and there will be no more crying or pain.
summary.older: The story ends where it began, with God and his people together, in a garden that has become a city. Jesus returns, death is undone, and God makes his home with people for ever.

sceneLabel: The garden that has become a city. A river as clear as crystal runs from the middle of the city down toward us, with a tree of life on each bank, heavy with fruit. The city wall has a gate standing open, and people from far away walk in along the road. There is no sun and no moon in the sky: the light shines from the centre of the city itself.

younger: The Bible's story began in a garden, with God and people together. It ends in a city that is also a garden, with God and people together again, for ever.

Jesus promised that he will come back. When he does, God will raise the dead to life, with new bodies that will never get sick or die again. God will judge the world fairly. Every wrong will be named and put right.
John saw a new heaven and a new earth, and he heard a loud voice say, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.” God will wipe away every tear. There will be no more death or crying or pain.

In the city a river as clear as crystal flows from God's throne, and a tree of life grows on each side of it. The gates are never shut. The city does not need the sun or the moon, because God's glory is its light. People from every nation bring their best gifts into it.

Christians do not know when Jesus will come back, and they understand some parts of Revelation in different ways. But they all believe he will come, that the dead will be raised, and that God will make everything new. That is a hope to wonder at, and to talk about with a parent, a pastor or a leader you trust.
older: Revelation was written by a prophet named John to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in cities where loyalty to Rome was shown by worshipping the emperor. It is written in pictures and symbols, many of them borrowed from the Old Testament, and its last two chapters bring the Bible's first chapters home: a river, the tree of life, no more curse, and God living with his people.

Christians confess together what the creeds confess: Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and there will be ‘the resurrection of the body; and the life everlasting’. Paul calls the risen Jesus “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20): his rising is the first part of a harvest still to come. The body that is buried “is raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42), and creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21). The hope is not that people escape the world. It is that God makes the world new.

God “has set a day when He will judge the world with justice” (Acts 17:31), and the dead are judged “according to their deeds” (Revelation 20:12). That is part of the hope, not a threat to hold over anyone: every wrong will be named, and those who suffered will not be forgotten. Christians confess a real judgment, and they differ on how to understand what it will be like. The site's Honest Answer on hell says, ‘The reality of judgment and of being finally separated from God is what the church has always taught, and it is close to the center of the faith. The exact nature and duration of hell is a different matter, and Bible-loving Christians have genuinely disagreed about it.’ And it adds, ‘Whatever hell is, it isn't what God wants for anyone.’

Then John sees “a new heaven and a new earth” and the holy city coming down from God, and he hears, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:1-3). There will be “no more death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). The city needs no sun, “because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp” (Revelation 21:23). Its gates are never shut, and “the glory and honor of the nations” is brought into it (Revelation 21:25-26). A river “as clear as crystal” flows from the throne, a tree of life stands on either side, and “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:1-3). God's people “will see His face” (Revelation 22:4).

This is not a story told to frighten anyone into believing. It is the end the whole road has been walking toward, offered for wonder: the God who walked in the garden will live with his people, face to face, in a world made new.

god.younger: God finishes what he starts. He will make everything new, and he wants to live with his people for ever.
god.older: God does not throw his world away; he makes it new: “Behold, I make all things new” (Revelation 21:5). He is just, and he will set every wrong right. And the end of the story is what he wanted from the first page: to live with his people, and for them to see his face.

verses.text: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God.
Behold, I make all things new.

differ.text: Where Christians differ. Christians who love the Bible read the order and timing of the last events in different ways: what the thousand years of Revelation 20 mean, whether Jesus will gather his people before a time of great trouble (some call this the rapture), and how the last events fit together. Faithful readers have held more than one view since the early church, and this stop does not choose between them. “No one knows about that day or hour” (Matthew 24:36), and Revelation is not a code for reading the news.
differ.label: The end-times study guide sets out each view at full strength.

care: This stop talks about death and about God's judgment. If you are grieving someone who has died, or if thinking about death or judgment makes you afraid, you do not have to carry that alone. Talk with a parent, a pastor or a leader you trust, or look at Find Help.

question.ask: Is heaven just floating on clouds for ever?
answer: No. That picture is common, but it is not the Bible's. The Bible's last pages do not show people leaving the world for the sky. They show “a new heaven and a new earth” and a city “coming down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:1-2). God's home comes to earth; people do not escape from it.

Paul says creation itself “will be set free from its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21), and that the body “is raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:42). The risen Jesus told his friends to touch him, and he ate a piece of fish in front of them (Luke 24:39-43). Christians confess ‘the resurrection of the body’, not a soul floating free.

Christians also believe that those who die trusting Jesus are with him now. Paul wrote of the desire “to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed” (Philippians 1:23). But that is not the end of the hope. The end is a whole world made new, with rivers and trees and nations, risen people, and God at the centre of it.

talk.younger: God will wipe away every tear. What is one thing you are looking forward to in God's new world? Who could you talk to about it?
talk.older: The Bible ends with a city full of nations and a world made new, not with an escape. How does that change the way you think about this world, and about the people in it?

activity.title: The end of the road is the beginning, made new
activity.prompt: Four pictures from the Bible's first pages come back on its last pages. Match each picture from Genesis to what Revelation says about it, then check.
